params.title: Installation, Maintenance & Repair
params.subtitle: Read a faulty radar display, find the suspect circuit, and install, maintain and service the radar safely.

onScreen: Installation, Maintenance & Repair
Symptom, then suspect: radar faults, maintenance, installation and safety
scenes.narration: This lesson is about keeping a radar working. First we'll read the symptoms a faulty radar shows on its display and on its meters, and match each one to the circuit to suspect. Then we'll cover maintenance, installation and safety. Listen for the pattern: symptom, then suspect. Most symptoms show up on the PPI, the plan position indicator, which is the round radar display.

params.title: A blank center that shrinks on longer ranges
labels: No target video in the center of the display
The blank spot gets smaller as the range scale is increased
Front panel control to check: the STC, set too high
Most likely defective area: a worn TR (TRL) cell

onScreen: No target video in the center
Blank spot shrinks on longer range scales
Check the STC control
Suspect a worn TR (TRL) cell
scenes.narration: Our first symptom. There's no target video in the center of the display, and the blank spot gets smaller as you increase the range scale. Something is blanking a fixed distance around your ship, and a fixed distance looks smaller on a longer range scale. The operator front panel control to check is the STC, the sensitivity time control. Set too high, it blanks all close-in video. For the same symptom, the most likely defective area is the TR cell, the transmit-receive cell, listed on the exam as the TR or TRL cell. A worn TR cell recovers slowly after the transmit pulse and keeps the receiver blocked for a fixed time, so nothing appears within a fixed distance of center.

params.title: Symptom, then suspect
rows: Oval range rings on the PPI
Sweep generation circuit
Rings are round only with equal sweeps
Docked: pier bends concave near center
Waveguide compensation delay line
Timing starts as the pulse leaves the antenna

onScreen: Oval range rings: sweep generation circuit
Pier bends concave near center: waveguide compensation delay line
scenes.narration: Next, the shape of what you see. If the range rings on the PPI are oval, suspect the sweep generation circuit. The rings are circular only when the horizontal and vertical deflection sweeps have equal amplitude. Now picture your ship docked. The pier appears distorted near the center of the PPI, bending in a concave fashion. That's the primary sign that the waveguide compensation delay line needs adjusting. The delay line makes the display start timing when the pulse actually leaves the antenna.

params.title: Digital video faults
labels: A bright, wide ring at a fixed distance from center, on all digital ranges
Suspect the video storage RAM or shift register
Raster scan: video missing in a rectangular block means a memory area failure

onScreen: Transmitter operating normally
Bright, wide ring at a fixed distance on all digital ranges
Suspect video storage RAM or shift register
Rectangular block missing on a raster scan: memory area failure
scenes.narration: Now a radar using digital video processing. The transmitter is operating normally, but a bright, wide ring appears at a fixed distance from center on all digital ranges. Suspect the video storage RAM, or random access memory, or the shift register. A stuck bit or a faulty memory location repeats the same ring at the same place on every range. Memory also explains the next symptom. On a raster scan display, if video is missing in a rectangular block, the most likely problem is a memory area failure, because each block of video memory maps to an area of the screen.

callouts.label: Point A: 200 kΩ input resistor
Point B: 100 kΩ input resistor
Point C: 50 kΩ input resistor
Point D: 25 kΩ input resistor
Feedback resistor R<sub>F</sub> = 10 kΩ
All inputs meet at the inverting input; the output is point E

onScreen: Point A: 200 kΩ
Point B: 100 kΩ
Point C: 50 kΩ
Point D: 25 kΩ
Feedback resistor R F = 10 kΩ
Output at point E
scenes.narration: Now some troubleshooting with a circuit card. Figure 8F12 is an inverting summing amplifier. Point A feeds a 200 kilohm resistor, point B a 100 kilohm resistor, point C a 50 kilohm resistor, and point D a 25 kilohm resistor. The exam calls them the 200 K, 100 K, 50 K and 25 K resistors. All 4 meet at the inverting input of the operational amplifier, or op amp. The feedback resistor, R sub F, is 10 kilohms, and the output is at point E.

params.title: Point E with 5 volts at B and C
steps: B and C at 5 V; A and D at zero volts
V<sub>out</sub> = −10 kΩ × (5 V/100 kΩ + 5 V/50 kΩ)

onScreen: V out = −R F × Σ(V/R)
B and C at 5 V, A and D at zero volts
V out = −1.5 V at point E
scenes.narration: To find the voltage at point E, use the summing amplifier formula. V sub out equals minus R sub F, times the sum of each input voltage divided by its resistor. The minus sign is there because the amplifier inverts. Say there are 5 volts at points B and C, and zero volts at points A and D. The zero-volt inputs add no current. 5 volts over 100 kilohms is 0.05 milliamps, and 5 volts over 50 kilohms is 0.1 milliamps. Multiply their sum by 10 kilohms and flip the sign. The voltage at point E is minus 1.5 volts.

params.title: After a card swap: −4.75 V at point E
steps: −10 kΩ × 0.375 mA = −3.75 V, the normal reading
params.answer: −4.75 V: the 50 K was replaced with a 25 K

onScreen: All inputs at 5 V
Normal: 0.375 mA, so −3.75 V
50 K replaced by 25 K: 0.475 mA
−4.75 V: the 50 K resistor became a 25 K
scenes.narration: Now a real fault. A circuit card has just been replaced with a spare, and with all inputs at 5 volts, point E reads minus 4.75 volts. What should it read? The input currents are 0.025, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 milliamps, a total of 0.375 milliamps. Times 10 kilohms, inverted, that's minus 3.75 volts, the normal reading. So the card draws extra current. If the 50 K resistor at point C was mistakenly replaced with a 25 K resistor, its current doubles to 0.2 milliamps. The sum becomes 0.475 milliamps, and point E reads minus 4.75 volts, exactly what you measured. The 50 K resistor has been replaced with a 25 K.

params.title: More symptoms, more suspects
rows: Bright flashing pie sections on the PPI
Defective crystal in the AFC section
AFC loses lock and hunts as the antenna turns
Sectors of solid video (spoking)
First check: interference from nearby ships
Their radars on a similar frequency
Range to a lighthouse is in error
Range ring oscillator
Its frequency sets the range ring spacing
TR tube malfunctions
The receiver might be damaged
Pulse energy can burn out the crystal mixer

onScreen: Flashing pie sections: defective AFC crystal
Spoking: check for interference from nearby ships
Lighthouse range error: range ring oscillator
TR tube malfunction: receiver might be damaged
scenes.narration: More pairs to learn. Bright, flashing pie sections on the PPI come from a defective crystal in the AFC, or automatic frequency control, section. The AFC loses lock and hunts, swinging the receiver tuning in and out as the antenna rotates. Sectors of solid video, called spoking, have a different first check: interference from nearby ships, whose radars on a similar frequency are a frequent cause. If the indicated distance to a lighthouse is in error, suspect the range ring oscillator, whose frequency sets the range ring spacing. And if the TR tube malfunctions, the receiver might be damaged, because high-power pulse energy reaches the crystal mixer and can burn it out.

params.title: Checking a mixer crystal with an ohmmeter

callouts.label: Silicon crystals are used in radar mixer and detector stages
Leads one way: low resistance
Leads reversed: high resistance in the opposite direction
Low one way, high the other: it's a working diode

onScreen: Silicon crystals in mixer and detector stages
Low resistance one way
High resistance with the leads reversed
Low one way, high the other: functional
scenes.narration: Silicon crystals are used in radar mixer and detector stages. How do you check one with an ohmmeter? A crystal is a diode, so it should conduct one way and block the other. Put the leads across it, and a functional crystal shows low resistance in one direction. Reverse the leads, and it shows high resistance in the opposite direction. Low one way, high the other: the crystal is good.

blocks.label: TR cell
blocks.note: Failure: low or no mixer current

onScreen: Antenna, TR cell and magnetron
Local oscillator and crystal mixer feed the IF amplifier
Small targets lost: magnetron, IF amplifier or receiver tuning
Low mixer current: local oscillator, TR cell or mixer diode
scenes.narration: Here's the receive path. Echoes from the antenna pass through the TR cell, which guards the receiver from the magnetron's transmit pulse. The local oscillator drives the crystal mixer, which converts the echoes to the IF, or intermediate frequency, for the IF amplifier. If the radar is not receiving small targets, the most likely causes are the magnetron, the IF amplifier, or receiver tuning, because anything that cuts transmitted power or receiver sensitivity loses weak echoes first. Now mixer current. It's local oscillator drive, rectified by the mixer diode. So low or no mixer current could be caused by any of these: local oscillator frequency misadjustment, TR cell failure, or mixer diode degradation.

params.title: Crystal replacement and magnetron current
items: Defective crystal mixer? Replace the crystal and the TR tube, not the ATR tube or klystron
A faulty TR tube usually caused the failure and would burn out a new crystal the same way
Magnetron current up while power output falls: the external magnetic field is weakening
A simply high magnetron current also means a defective external magnetic field
Weak field: electrons go straight to the anode instead of spiraling past the cavities

onScreen: Bad crystal mixer: replace the crystal and the TR tube
A faulty TR tube would burn out a new crystal
Current up, power down: weakening magnet
High magnetron current: defective magnetic field
Electrons go straight to the anode
scenes.narration: When the crystal mixer becomes defective, replace the crystal and the TR tube. Not the ATR, or anti-transmit-receive, tube, and not the klystron. A faulty TR tube usually caused the failure, and it would burn out a new crystal the same way. Next, the magnetron current meter. An increase in magnetron current that coincides with a decrease in power output, or simply a high magnetron current, indicates a weakening or defective external magnetic field. With a weak magnet, more electrons go straight to the anode instead of spiraling past the cavities, so current rises while useful output drops.

callouts.label: External magnet: makes electrons spiral past the cavities
Weaker field: more electrons go straight from cathode to anode
Current meter rises: suspect a decrease in magnetic field strength
Lower duty cycle or weaker modulator pulse: less current, not more
No magnetic field at all: no oscillation, excessive current, tube destroyed

onScreen: Magnet makes electrons spiral past the cavities
Weaker field: electrons go straight to the anode
Current meter rises: magnetic field decreasing
Lower duty cycle or weaker pulse: less current
No magnetic field: it destroys itself
scenes.narration: Here's why the magnetron current meter matters. The external magnet makes electrons spiral past the cavities on their way from cathode to anode. If the field weakens, more electrons go straight to the anode. So an increase in the deflection on the magnetron current meter is likely caused by a decrease of the magnetic field strength. A lower duty cycle or a weaker modulator pulse would work the other way: they reduce the current, not increase it. And if the magnetron is allowed to operate without its magnetic field in place, electrons rush straight from cathode to anode with no oscillation, and it will quickly destroy itself from excessive current flow.

params.title: Radar bearing versus visual bearing
labels: The radar shows the target on this bearing
The visual bearing to the same target doesn't agree
First suspect: incorrect antenna position information
Check the synchro, resolver or encoder signals and the heading alignment

onScreen: Radar bearing of the target
Visual bearing doesn't agree
Suspect incorrect antenna position information
Synchro, resolver or encoder signals and heading alignment
scenes.narration: Next symptom: targets on the radar display are not on the same bearing as their visual bearing. Here the echo sits on one bearing, but your line of sight to the same target says another. What should you suspect first? Incorrect antenna position information. The display can only place an echo correctly if it knows where the antenna is pointing. So check the antenna position signals from the synchro, resolver or encoder, and the heading alignment.

params.title: From the magnetron to the array termination

onScreen: Magnetron, waveguide, rotary joint
Wet weather loses distant targets: leak in waveguide or rotary joint
High VSWR means reflected energy
Array termination absorbs what the slots don't radiate
Slotted array
scenes.narration: Follow the energy from the magnetron through the waveguide and the rotary joint. If you lose distant targets during and immediately after wet weather, suspect a leak in the waveguide or rotary joint. Water gets in and attenuates the signal until it dries out. Now a high VSWR, or voltage standing wave ratio, at the magnetron output. That means energy is reflecting back. If the waveguide and rotary joint appear to work properly, suspect the waveguide array termination. It's the matched load at the end of the slotted array that absorbs the energy the slots don't radiate. When it fails, that energy reflects back down the guide.

params.title: Equipment faults: symptom, then suspect
rows: Magnetron current meter rises
Decrease in magnetic field strength
Targets off their visual bearing
Antenna position information
Distant targets lost after wet weather
Leak in waveguide or rotary joint
High VSWR; waveguide and joint OK
Waveguide array termination
2 radars, different ranges to a target
Sweep and timing circuits of both indicators

onScreen: Current meter rises: weaker magnetic field
Off visual bearing: antenna position information
Wet weather: waveguide or rotary joint leak
High VSWR: array termination
2 radars disagree on range: check sweep and timing of both
scenes.narration: Let's line up this topic's faults, and add a new one at the end. A rising magnetron current meter: a weaker magnetic field. Targets off their visual bearing: antenna position information. Distant targets lost after wet weather: a leak in the waveguide or rotary joint. High VSWR with a good waveguide and rotary joint: the array termination. And the new one. When 2 radars on one vessel show different ranges to the same target, check the sweep and timing circuits of both indicators for correct readings, to find which one is wrong. Don't average the readings. Averaging would just spread the error.

params.title: Water in the waveguide
labels: Large circular rings near the center
The water reflects pulse energy back into the receiver

onScreen: Ordinary echoes
Large circular rings near the center
Water in the waveguide
Pulse energy reflected into the receiver
scenes.narration: Now maintenance, starting with what the display tells you. Alongside the ordinary echoes, this display shows large circular rings near the center. That's the sign of water in the waveguide. The water reflects pulse energy straight back into the receiver, and those reflections paint the rings. So large rings near the center mean water inside the guide.

params.title: Maintenance rules
items: Thick rust and corrosion on a parabolic dish: lower performance, especially for weak targets
Keep the waveguide's interior surface as clean as possible to minimize signal loss
Echo box: tests and tunes the radar by providing artificial targets
Replacing the magnetron? Always use a non-magnetic screwdriver

onScreen: Rusty dish: lower performance on weak targets
Keep the waveguide interior clean
Echo box: artificial targets for testing and tuning
Non-magnetic screwdriver for the magnetron
scenes.narration: A few maintenance rules. Thick rust and corrosion on the surface of a parabolic dish cause a decrease in performance, especially for weak targets, because they reduce antenna gain on transmit and receive. Keep the interior surface of a waveguide as clean as possible to minimize signal loss. Skin effect puts the microwave current on that surface, so paint or oil would only add loss. The echo box is used for testing and tuning the radar by providing artificial targets. It's a high-Q resonant cavity that stores energy from the transmitted pulse and rings it back to the receiver. And always use a non-magnetic screwdriver when replacing the magnetron. Its strong permanent magnet can yank a steel tool, damaging the tube or injuring your hand, and magnetic tools can weaken the magnet.

params.title: The most useful radar servicing instrument

callouts.label: The oscilloscope: most useful instrument for radar servicing
Shows the shape, amplitude and timing of a waveform
Probe the pulses, the video and the sweep waveforms

onScreen: Oscilloscope: most useful for radar servicing
Shape, amplitude and timing
Pulses, video and sweep waveforms
scenes.narration: Which instrument is most useful for radar servicing? The oscilloscope. Radar work is all about pulses and timing, and the oscilloscope shows you the shape, amplitude and timing of the waveforms you need to check: the pulses, the video, and the sweep waveforms. A frequency counter, a wattmeter or an audio generator can't show you those waveforms.

params.title: S-band: coax or waveguide?
rows: Losses kept reasonable at S-band
Large and heavy
Lower installation cost
Costly to install

onScreen: Coax: losses kept reasonable at S-band
Coax: lower installation cost
S-band waveguide: large, heavy and costly
scenes.narration: On to installation. Why is coaxial cable often used for S-band installations instead of waveguide? Because losses can be kept reasonable at S-band frequencies, and the installation cost is lower. S-band waveguide is large, heavy and costly to run. Coax does the job for less.

blocks.label: Waveguide run
blocks.note: As straight and vertical as possible

blocks.label: Extra bends and twists
blocks.note: Each can cause reflections and distortion

onScreen: Transceiver, straight waveguide, antenna
Avoid long horizontal runs: condensation
Avoid bends and twists: reflections and distortion
scenes.narration: Next, the waveguide run from the transceiver up to the antenna. The ideal run is straight and mostly vertical. Avoid long horizontal runs of waveguide to prevent accumulation of condensation. Moisture can collect in a horizontal section with nowhere to drain, where it absorbs RF, or radio frequency, energy and corrodes the walls. And install waveguides as straight as possible to reduce distortion, since every bend or twist can cause reflections.

callouts.label: Most important: a location not shadowed by other structures
Masts and funnels in the beam create blind sectors
Height, run length and maintenance access come second
Properly ground, bond and shield all units to stop receiver interference

onScreen: Not shadowed by other structures: most important
Masts and funnels create blind sectors
Height, run length and access come second
Ground, bond and shield all units
scenes.narration: Where should the antenna go? The most important factor is a location that is not shadowed by other structures. Masts and funnels in the beam's path create blind sectors where targets can't be seen. Height, the length of the run, and easy maintenance access all come second. And another installation rule: radar interference to a communications receiver is eliminated by properly grounding, bonding and shielding all units, which keeps the pulse energy contained.

params.title: ESD damage: now or much later

badges.label: Hidden damage
badges.note: At a time when the radar set is critically needed

badges.label: Discharges too small to feel
badges.note: You may never notice it happened

onScreen: ESD: immediate failure
ESD: failure much later, when critically needed
Discharges too small to feel can do it
scenes.narration: Last topic: safety, starting with ESD, which stands for electrostatic discharge. ESD damage may cause immediate circuit failures. But it may also cause failures much later, at times when the radar set is critically needed. And discharges too small to feel can do it, so you may never know the damage happened.

params.title: Before you start work
rows: Handle solid state circuit boards
Proper work surfaces and ESD straps in place
Test a radar transmitter
No explosives or flammable cargo being loaded
Repair or adjust a radar unit
High-voltage capacitors discharged to ground

onScreen: Boards: ESD straps and proper work surfaces
Transmitter test: no explosives or flammable cargo being loaded
Repairs: discharge high-voltage capacitors to ground
scenes.narration: Before removing, servicing or making measurements on any solid state circuit boards, make sure the proper work surfaces and ESD grounding straps are in place. Before testing a radar transmitter, make sure there are no explosives or flammable cargo being loaded, since radiated energy can fire electrically initiated explosives or ignite flammable vapors. And while making repairs or adjustments to radar units, discharge all high-voltage capacitors to ground. They can hold lethal charges after the power is removed.

params.title: Handling a CRT
items: Removing a CRT from its operating casing: wear gloves and goggles
A cracked envelope can implode and throw glass
A dropped CRT might implode, causing damage to workers and equipment

onScreen: Removing a CRT: gloves and goggles
Cracked envelope can implode
Dropped CRT might implode
scenes.narration: Radar displays may use a CRT, a cathode ray tube. While removing a CRT from its operating casing, wear gloves and goggles, because a cracked envelope can implode and throw glass. And handle it with care: if a CRT is dropped, it might implode, causing damage to workers and equipment. That's the end of this lesson. Remember the pattern, symptom then suspect, and put safety first.
